messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 37-year-old psychologist who was raped two years ago by a male colleague during a national conference. The attack occurred in a locked hotel room after a late-night workshop; the colleague had cornered him, and Kwame froze, certain he could not stop what was happening. In the months that followed, he came to believe that the event had fundamentally damaged him—that he had no future, that kindness from others only masked hidden danger, and that anyone who looked at him could see exactly what had happened.

These negative appraisals fueled a constant, low-grade threat monitoring. Because he felt exposed and helpless, Kwame began checking every room before he entered it. At work—he still sees clients in a small office—he always chooses the seat with his back against the wall, facing the door, so no one can approach unseen. He cannot relax, even when he knows a place is safe; his body stays tense, his gaze scanning. Sleep is difficult: he lies alert for hours, listening for footsteps or the click of a lock, because dropping his guard feels like inviting disaster.

The same appraisals sharpened the world into a field of triggers. Being alone with any man now feels dangerous—the memory of the assailant's weight and voice floods back. He now schedules his clients so that the last session ends before evening, when the building empties and corridors go quiet. Comments about sexual violence, even in casual conversation among colleagues, make him flinch; he cuts off discussions, certain the speaker will turn to him and see. Locked doors are the worst. A therapy-room door that clicks shut makes his heart race; he has started propping it open with a chair, and when a client once closed it fully, he had to excuse himself, trembling.

The hypervigilance itself deepened his helplessness. Each time his body reacted—darting eyes, clenched jaw, racing pulse—he felt proof that he was still a victim, still unable to stop bad things from happening. This made the triggers even more potent. A male receptionist leaning into his office to ask a question now sent him into a cold sweat, as if the locked-room memory were being re-enacted. He began avoiding the break room and stopped attending staff meetings; his supervisor noticed his absences but Kwame could not explain.

His daily environment as a psychologist became a minefield. The very spaces built for healing—quiet, enclosed, one-on-one—mirrored the scene of the assault. He felt that his own office was turning against him. The belief that others could read his trauma in his face became unbearable; he avoided eye contact with clients, certain they would see shame in his eyes. Helplessness spread: he stopped applying for conference travel, stopped dating, stopped hosting friends. The future he had imagined as a competent professional felt gone.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a single, mundane incident. A new client, a tall man, closed the door to the therapy room and sat down. Kwame felt his breath disappear, his back exposed. He ended the session early, apologized, and then sat alone in the car park for an hour, unable to drive. That night he admitted to himself that he could no longer live this way—always watching, always afraid, always seeing his own violation in the faces of others. He is terrified that therapy will force him to relive the rape, but more terrified that without it, his life will keep shrinking until there is nothing left but the locked room.
